```{r setup, include=FALSE}
options(htmltools.dir.version = FALSE)
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(patchwork)
library(ggrepel)
library(palmerpenguins)
library(gganimate)
library(plotly)
library(magick)
```

## Outline of class

Advanced plotting techniques for creating publication-ready visualizations

::: {.incremental}
1. [patchwork]{.fn} — bringing plots together
2. [ggrepel]{.fn} — repel your labels on your plots
3. [gganimate]{.fn} — add smooth animations to your plots
4. [plotly]{.fn} — create interactive animated plots
5. [magick]{.fn} — photo processing
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Exploration Required
This is just a taste of what each package can do. Check out the documentation for each to delve deeper!
:::

---

## Install new packages

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
install.packages("patchwork")  # for bringing plots together
install.packages("ggrepel")    # for repelling labels
install.packages("gganimate")  # smooth animations
install.packages("gifski")     # for saving gifs
install.packages("plotly")     # for interactive animations
install.packages("magick")     # for images
```

---

# Part 1: patchwork

---

## What is patchwork?

[patchwork]{.fn} makes it easy to bring your plots together with simple operations.

![](https://cdn.myportfolio.com/45214904-6a61-4e23-98d6-b140f8654a40/74f015a1-4d22-4b59-9fd0-69ca676d3f05_rw_3840.png?h=6324d466abdfbb47aa0094a270a508d2){fig-align="center" width="70%"}

---

## Create two simple plots

Using the Palmer penguin dataset:

```{r}
#| echo: true
p1 <- penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = body_mass_g, 
             y = bill_length_mm, 
             color = species)) +
  geom_point()

p1
```

---

## Create the second plot

```{r}
#| echo: true
p2 <- penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sex, 
             y = body_mass_g, 
             color = species)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2)

p2
```

---

## Combine plots with [+]{.op}

```{r}
#| echo: true
p1 + p2
```

---

## Collect legends

```{r}
#| echo: true
p1 + p2 +
  plot_layout(guides = 'collect')
```

---

## Add labels (A, B, etc.)

```{r}
#| echo: true
p1 + p2 +
  plot_layout(guides = 'collect') +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = 'A')
```

---

## Stack plots vertically with [/]{.op}

```{r}
#| echo: true
p1 / p2 +
  plot_layout(guides = 'collect') +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = 'A')
```

---

## Learn more about patchwork

[patchwork]{.fn} has many cool ways to arrange and modify plots.

For more information, see the [patchwork vignettes](https://patchwork.data-imaginist.com/articles/patchwork.html).

![](https://repository-images.githubusercontent.com/112388106/6e5a3600-6547-11e9-84f6-3656ac797821){fig-align="center" width="60%"}

# Part 2: ggrepel

---

## Clear labels with ggrepel

[ggrepel]{.fn} makes it easy to add clear, non-overlapping labels to your plots.

![](https://cdn.myportfolio.com/45214904-6a61-4e23-98d6-b140f8654a40/874dedf0-55d1-4cdd-a390-45b8376d2fc2_rw_1920.png?h=39c69f525af3256f7096f510bafb0913){fig-align="center" width="60%"}

---

## mtcars dataset

We'll use the built-in [mtcars]{.var} dataset (car specifications):

```{r}
#| echo: true
head(mtcars)
```

---

## Plot without label repelling

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, 
                   y = mpg, 
                   label = rownames(mtcars))) +
  geom_text() +
  geom_point(color = 'red')
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, 
                   y = mpg, 
                   label = rownames(mtcars))) +
  geom_text() +
  geom_point(color = 'red')
```

:::

:::

Notice the labels are overlapping!

---

## Repel the labels with [geom_text_repel()]{.fn}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, 
                   y = mpg, 
                   label = rownames(mtcars))) +
  geom_text_repel() +
  geom_point(color = 'red')
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, 
                   y = mpg, 
                   label = rownames(mtcars))) +
  geom_text_repel() +
  geom_point(color = 'red')
```

:::

:::

Much clearer!

---

## Use [geom_label_repel()]{.fn} for boxes

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, 
                   y = mpg, 
                   label = rownames(mtcars))) +
  geom_label_repel() +
  geom_point(color = 'red')
```

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = wt, 
                   y = mpg, 
                   label = rownames(mtcars))) +
  geom_label_repel() +
  geom_point(color = 'red')
```

:::

:::

Adds boxes around the labels for better readability.

---

## Learn more about ggrepel

For more cool things you can do with [ggrepel]{.fn}, see the [examples here](https://ggrepel.slowkow.com/articles/examples.html).

# Part 3: gganimate

---

## Bring your plots to life

[gganimate]{.fn} lets you create animations that show data changing over time or groups.

![](https://repository-images.githubusercontent.com/50872540/14597080-6547-11e9-9821-271c29481839){fig-align="center" width="60%"}

---

## Static penguin plot

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = body_mass_g, 
             y = bill_depth_mm, 
             color = species)) +
  geom_point()
```

---

## Add transition with [transition_states()]{.fn}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="45%"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| warning: false
penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = body_mass_g, 
             y = bill_depth_mm, 
             color = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  transition_states(
    year,
    transition_length = 2,
    state_length = 1
  )
```

:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
p <- penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = body_mass_g, 
             y = bill_depth_mm, 
             color = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  transition_states(
    year,
    transition_length = 2,
    state_length = 1
  )
animate(p, nframes = 75, renderer = gifski_renderer(), fps = 10)
```

:::

:::

---

## Add a dynamic title with [labs()]{.fn}

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="45%"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = body_mass_g, 
             y = bill_depth_mm, 
             color = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  transition_states(year, 
                    transition_length = 2, 
                    state_length = 1) +
  labs(title = 'Year: {closest_state}')
```

:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
p <- penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = body_mass_g, 
             y = bill_depth_mm, 
             color = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  transition_states(year, 
                    transition_length = 2, 
                    state_length = 1) +
  labs(title = 'Year: {closest_state}')
animate(p, nframes = 75, renderer = gifski_renderer(), fps = 10)
```

:::

:::

The placeholder [{closest_state}]{.param} updates with each frame.

---

## Save animation as GIF with [anim_save()]{.fn}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
p<-penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = body_mass_g, 
             y = bill_depth_mm, 
             color = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  transition_states(year, 
                    transition_length = 2, 
                    state_length = 1) +
  ease_aes("sine-in-out") +
  labs(title = 'Year: {closest_state}') 
  anim_save(here("Week_05", "output", "penguin_animation.gif"), animation = p)
```

---

## Learn more about gganimate

For more advanced animations, see the [gganimate documentation](https://gganimate.com/index.html).

# Part 4: plotly

---

## Interactive animations with plotly

[plotly]{.fn} creates interactive plots with built-in animation that respond to user input. Perfect for exploratory data analysis!

![](https://plotly.com/all_static/images/logo-white.svg){fig-align="center" width="40%"}

---

## Create an interactive scatter plot

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| warning: false


penguins |>
  plot_ly(x = ~body_mass_g,
          y = ~bill_depth_mm,
          color = ~species,
          type = "scatter",
          mode = "markers") |>
  layout(title = "Penguin Body Mass vs Bill Depth",
         xaxis = list(title = "Body Mass (g)"),
         yaxis = list(title = "Bill Depth (mm)"))
```

---
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
library(plotly)

penguins |>
  plot_ly(x = ~body_mass_g,
          y = ~bill_depth_mm,
          color = ~species,
          type = "scatter",
          mode = "markers") |>
  layout(title = "Penguin Body Mass vs Bill Depth",
         xaxis = list(title = "Body Mass (g)"),
         yaxis = list(title = "Bill Depth (mm)"))
```
::: {.callout-note}
## Hover for details
Plotly plots are interactive! Hover over points to see exact values, zoom in/out, and pan around.
:::

---

## Animate by species with frame

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
penguins |>
  plot_ly(x = ~body_mass_g,
          y = ~bill_depth_mm,
          frame = ~species,
          color = ~species,
          type = "scatter",
          mode = "markers",
          marker = list(size = 8)) |>
  layout(title = "Penguin Characteristics by Species",
         xaxis = list(title = "Body Mass (g)"),
         yaxis = list(title = "Bill Depth (mm)"))
```

Click the play button to animate through species!

---

## Advantages of plotly over gganimate

::: {.incremental}
- **Interactive** — hover, zoom, pan, click to explore
- **Easier syntax** — less code than gganimate
- **Web-ready** — works in HTML, Shiny, dashboards
- **3D capable** — can create 3D scatter plots and surfaces
- **No rendering** — animations happen in the browser, not rendered as GIFs
:::

---

## Learn more about plotly

For more interactive visualization options, see the [plotly R documentation](https://plotly.com/r/).

# Part 5: magick

---

## Advanced image processing

[magick]{.fn} lets you read, process, and composite images programmatically.

![](https://jeroen.github.io/images/magick.png){fig-align="center" width="60%"}

---

## Read an image with [image_read()]{.fn}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
penguin <- image_read("https://pngimg.com/uploads/penguin/pinguin_PNG9.png")

penguin
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## SSL/TLS errors?
If you get an SSL/TLS error, [follow this solution](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/64147821/error-running-weathercan-package-fatal-ssl-tls-alert-e-g-handshake-failed).
:::

---

## Save a plot as an image

First, create and save your plot:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
penguinplot<-penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = body_mass_g, 
             y = bill_depth_mm, 
             color = species)) +
  geom_point() 
  ggsave(here("Week_05", "output", "penguinplot.png"))
  penguinplot
```

---

## Composite images with [image_composite()]{.fn}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
penplot <- image_read(here("Week_05", "output", "penguinplot.png"))
out <- image_composite(image = penplot,       composite_image = penguin, offset = "+70+30")
out
```

Creates a composite image with the penguin placed at coordinates (70, 30).

---

## Animate composite images

You can combine GIFs with images too:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
pengif <- image_read("https://media3.giphy.com/media/H4uE6w9G1uK4M/giphy.gif")
outgif <- image_composite(penplot, pengif, gravity = "center")
animation <- image_animate(outgif, fps = 10, optimize = TRUE)
animation
```

---

## Learn more about magick

For more advanced image processing, see the [magick vignette](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/magick/vignettes/intro.html).

![](https://ropensci.org/blog/2017/11/07/magick-knitr/0E5cqaz.png){fig-align="center" width="60%"}
